\chapter{El Cuarto Y La Mesa --- Key, Shower, Table, Light, Bathroom}
\label{ch:el-cuarto-y-la-mesa}
\hlchaptermodality{310}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask a stranger in Spanish for the five things a room and a table make me ask for: the key, the shower, the table, the light and the bathroom.}

Complete ES-C310-bano: ask for all five, ending with the question every traveller needs first --- donde esta el bano.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la llave]{la llave — the little key, and the three English words hiding it}

\label{lesson:ES-C310-llave}



\begin{quote}
Two repairs from last time, before anything new is added. Which one admits you have no answer? (\emph{No sé}.) Which one asks a stranger for a meaning? (\emph{¿Qué significa?})
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{LLA-ve}, stress on the first part. The \emph{ll} is a \emph{y}, so this begins the way \emph{yes} begins. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la llave} — \textquotedblleft{}the key.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{clavis} was the key. Spanish softened the \emph{cl-} into that \emph{ll-}, the same way \emph{clamare} became \emph{llamar}, and the shape of the old word all but disappeared. English never softened it, so English is where you can still see it.

Look at your collarbone. It is the \textbf{clavicle} — the \emph{little key} — because a Roman anatomist thought it turned like one where it meets the shoulder. Look at the start of a line of music: that is the \textbf{clef}, the key that unlocks which note each line means. And when cardinals are shut in a room to choose a pope, they are \emph{cum clave}, \textbf{with a key} — in \textbf{conclave}.

Three English words, one Spanish word, one Latin key. You have carried \emph{clavis} around in your own shoulder your whole life.

Say \emph{la llave, por favor} at a hotel desk and you will be handed one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of the things you have to ask a stranger for.

Everything in this run is an object that somebody else is holding, and the only way to it is a question. That is why these words sit with your repair kit rather than apart from it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la llave}
  \item \emph{la llave, por favor}
  \item \emph{disculpe — la llave, por favor}
  \item \emph{no sé. ¿qué significa?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which bone is named \textquotedblleft{}the little key\textquotedblright{}? (The \emph{clavicle}.) What is \emph{la llave}? (The key.) And which two repairs opened this lesson? (\emph{No sé} and \emph{¿qué significa?})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la ducha]{la ducha — a thing that leads water}

\label{lesson:ES-C310-ducha}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. Which English bone is the \emph{little key}? (The \emph{clavicle}, from the same \emph{clavis} as \emph{llave}.) And which question earns you a meaning from a stranger? (\emph{¿Qué significa?})
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{DU-cha}, stress on the first part. The \emph{d} is soft, closer to the \emph{th} of \emph{this} than to an English \emph{d}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la ducha} — \textquotedblleft{}the shower.\textquotedblright{}

Spanish borrowed this one from Italian \emph{doccia}, a pipe or a spout, and Italian had it from Latin \textbf{ducere}: \textbf{to lead}.

That is the whole idea. A shower is not named for water and not named for washing. It is named for the fact that something \textbf{leads} the water to where you are standing.

\emph{Ducere} is one of the busiest roots English owns. A \textbf{duct} leads air. An \textbf{aqueduct} leads water — \emph{aqua} plus \emph{ducere}, and the Romans built them for five hundred years. To \textbf{conduct} is to lead together; to \textbf{introduce} is to lead somebody in; to \textbf{produce} is to lead a thing forward into the world. And a \textbf{duke} is a \emph{dux}, the one who leads.

A duke and a shower head, doing the same job.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two objects now, and both of them belong to somebody else.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la ducha}
  \item \emph{la llave}, then \emph{la ducha}
  \item \emph{disculpe, ¿dónde está la ducha?}
  \item \emph{¿qué significa?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{ducere} mean? (To lead.) So what does an aqueduct do to water? (Leads it.) Which English title is the plain \emph{dux}? (\emph{Duke}.) And what is \emph{la llave}? (The key.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la mesa]{la mesa — the one word English took without changing a letter}

\label{lesson:ES-C310-mesa}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. What is \emph{la llave}? (The key.) And what does a \emph{ducha} do, going by its root? (It leads the water to you.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ME-sa}, stress on the first part. The \emph{s} stays clear and hissed; it never buzzes into a \emph{z}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la mesa} — \textquotedblleft{}the table.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{mensa} was the table, and it sits next to \emph{metiri}, \textquotedblleft{}to measure.\textquotedblright{} A \emph{mensa} was a board \textbf{cut to a measure} — flat, level, and made so on purpose. Flatness is the whole of the word.

Which is why English has this one twice, and one of the two came the long way round. When English speakers reached the American southwest they found hills whose tops were sheared level, and they took the local Spanish word for it. A \textbf{mesa} in English is a flat-topped hill. It is \emph{la mesa} with nothing changed — not the spelling, not the sound, not the idea. A table is a small flat top; a mesa is an enormous one.

The Latin sense survives too, in \textbf{commensal}: creatures that are \emph{commensal} eat at one table.

\emph{Una mesa, por favor} gets you seated.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The key got you in, and the table is where the asking really starts.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la mesa}
  \item \emph{la mesa, por favor}
  \item \emph{la llave}, then \emph{la ducha}, then \emph{la mesa}
  \item \emph{disculpe, ¿dónde está la mesa?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a \emph{mesa} in English? (A flat-topped hill — the same word, untouched.) What did \emph{mensa} have to do with measuring? (It was a board cut to a measure.) And which of your three words leads water? (\emph{La ducha}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la luz]{la luz — the word that clears things up}

\label{lesson:ES-C310-luz}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. What does a \emph{ducha} lead? (Water.) And which English word is \emph{la mesa}, borrowed whole? (\emph{Mesa}, the flat-topped hill.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item One syllable: \emph{luz}. The final \emph{z} is an \emph{s} across the Americas and a \emph{th} in much of Spain, and both are correct where they are said. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la luz} — \textquotedblleft{}the light.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{lux} shows its fuller shape in the form \emph{lucem}, and that \emph{luc-} is what English borrowed, over and over.

Something \textbf{lucid} is lit from inside — clear enough to see through. Something \textbf{translucent} lets light \emph{across} it. To \textbf{elucidate} is to bring light \emph{out of} a thing, which is what a good explanation does. And the morning star was \textbf{Lucifer}, the \emph{light-bearer}, before the name was given to anybody else.

There is a second, older link that is easy to miss. English \textbf{light} is not borrowed from Latin at all — it came down the Germanic side of the family. But go back far enough and \emph{lux} and \emph{light} meet at one ancient root meaning brightness. The two words have been apart for thousands of years and still mean the same thing.

\emph{No hay luz} is what you say when the bulb is dead.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four objects, and this is the first one you ask about when it is missing rather than when you want it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la luz}
  \item \emph{no hay luz}
  \item \emph{disculpe — no hay luz. ayuda, por favor}
  \item \emph{la ducha}, then \emph{la mesa}, then \emph{la luz}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{elucidate} do, literally? (Brings light out of something.) Is English \emph{light} borrowed from \emph{lux}? (No — it is a distant cousin, not a loan.) And what is \emph{la mesa}? (The table.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el baño]{el baño — the question every traveller asks first}

\label{lesson:ES-C310-bano}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. What is \emph{la mesa}? (The table.) And what does \emph{elucidate} do to a thing? (Brings light out of it, from the same \emph{luc-} as \emph{luz}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{BA-ño}, stress on the first part. The \emph{ñ} is one sound, the \emph{ny} in \emph{canyon} — which is itself Spanish \emph{cañón}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el baño} — \textquotedblleft{}the bathroom.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{balneum} was the bath, and Latin had taken it from Greek \emph{balaneion}, the bath house. Spanish wore \emph{balneum} down to \emph{baño}: the \emph{l} fell out and the \emph{-ne-} folded into that single \emph{ñ}.

Now the trap, because it is worth naming. English \textbf{bath} looks like family. It is not. \emph{Bath} came down the Germanic side and never met \emph{balneum} at all. The honest English relative is the rare one: \textbf{balneology}, the study of baths and bathing waters, which is exactly \emph{balneum} with a Greek ending stuck on.

Two words for the same room, sitting side by side for centuries, unrelated. When a pair looks obvious, that is precisely when it pays to check.

\emph{¿Dónde está el baño?} is the sentence you will need before any other in this run, and you already have every piece of it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five things a room and a table make you ask for: the key, the shower, the table, the light, the bathroom. None of them are yours until somebody tells you where they are.

That is the chapter. Next comes the shop, where the asking costs money.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el baño}
  \item \emph{¿dónde está el baño?}
  \item \emph{disculpe, ¿dónde está el baño?}
  \item \emph{la mesa}, then \emph{la luz}, then \emph{el baño}
  \item \emph{gracias}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is English \emph{bath} related to \emph{baño}? (No — it only looks like it.) Which English word is the real relative? (\emph{Balneology}.) And say the whole question one more time. (\emph{¿Dónde está el baño?})
\end{tcolorbox}
